To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the bactericidal rate constant and the postantibioitc effect (PAE), measured simultaneously, are highly correlated (P < 0001) for each antibiotic tested, including tobramycin (aminoglycosides) and ciprofloxaxcin (quinolones) which bind irreversibly and tetracycine and trimethoprim (both bind reversibly), and that this correlation holds true when the data from the five antibiotics tested are considered together

(i) PAEs for all the five antibiotics studied increased nonlinearly and in a saturable way with increasing antibiotic concentrations, (ii) PAE correlated with bactericidal activity in a nonlinear and saturable fashion for each of the five antibiotic-bactericium combinations, and (iii) PAE correlated well with bactericidal rate constant for each antibiotic and also across the five antibiotics.

(i) bactericidal activity is a saturable function of antibiotic concentration, (ii) the PAE is also a saturable function, and (iii) PAEs and bacteriostatic rate constants correlate with each other for all antibiotic concentrations tested.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the relationship between PAE, a measure of antibiotic persistence, and bactericidal effect, a measure of the antibiotic-induced damage to bacterial cells, and it provides evidence that cellular recovery from sublethal damage may be a major factor determining the length of the PAE.
the relationship between PAE and bacteriocidal activity for five antibiotics with diverse mechanisms of action.
the relationship between PAE and bacteriolysis and the role of antibiotic binding in the mechanism of action of antimicrobial agents.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the degree of cellular damage inflicted by an antibiotic is the major determinant of the duration of the PAE for all antibiotics with different mechanisms and that binding of the antibiotics to bacterial receptors is not a determinant of the duration.
the degree of bacteriostatic or bactericidal activity for an antibiotic is a good predictor of the length of PAEs, especially if the antibiotic binds irreversibly to its receptors.

PAE is a function of the extent of bacterial recovery from nonlethally damaged cells following antibiotic exposure, which is determined by the binding characteristics of the antibiotic to its receptor.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, for antibiotics which bind to bacterial receptors irreversibly, the PAE may be used to predict the extent of cellular injury inflicted on bacteria by the antibiotic, and vice versa.

, for antibiotics with different mechanisms and different degrees of binding irreversibility, the extent of bacterial damage inflicted on bacteria, as reflected by the bactericidal rate constant, correlates well with the length of PAEs, suggesting that cellular recovery from sublethal damage may be an important determinant of the PAE.
the PAE is a measure of the duration of the cellular recovery period following nonlethal damage to bacterial cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the PAE reflects cellular recovery, not just the duration of cellular damage, which may have important implications for clinical practice and for future research on the mechanisms of PAE.
the PAE is a good measure of antibiotic potency, and it is an excellent predictor of antibiotic efficacy in vivo.
the extent of bacterial damage inflicted by an antibiotic may reflect the duration of PAE.
